ticket.body:
## In plain words

When someone files an issue about module imports in a Next.js or Vite project, fabrika's leak guard refuses the body because the project's tilde-slash import alias looks like a path into the user's home folder. That blocks honest bug reports in outside repos, and the only workarounds are rewording the alias or masking it, which ruins the repro. We would teach the guard to recognise the two code shapes an alias actually appears in, and keep refusing everything else exactly as today.

## Problem

`scanBody` in `packages/fabrika-cli/src/report/leaks.ts` is the body-surface leak predicate every writing verb shares (`report file`/`note`/`amend`, `triage enrich`/`kill`, the `build`/`review`/`ship` authored bodies, and more). Its `PATH_RE` treats the home marker `~` followed by one or more `/segment` runs as a `home-relative` path, with no look at what surrounds it. A tilde-slash path alias is source code, not a filesystem path, but it has exactly that shape, so it refuses on exit 5.

Triage note: reproduced at `origin/main` (39fe3530f) by calling `scanBody` directly. All five lines below came back `home-relative`. The first three are false positives; the last two are real home paths that must stay refused. The alias is written out in words here because this very guard would refuse the literal text in this issue body:

1. a tsconfig `paths` key: quoted tilde, slash, star, followed by a colon;
2. an import specifier: `from`, then a quoted tilde, slash, `components/Button`;
3. prose naming the alias in backticks: tilde, slash, `lib/utils`;
4. tilde, slash, `Documents/notes.txt`;
5. tilde, slash, `.config/foo`.

## Scope: exempt the code shapes, not a list of directory names

The shipped contract (`claude-plugins/fabrika/skills/report/contract.md`, section "The body-surface leak predicate") says the home-relative carve-outs are "pinned to a shape rather than a membership list". This fix follows that rule.

- **In scope: a module specifier.** A tilde-slash path that is the whole content of a matching quote pair (`"` or `'`) immediately after `from`, `import`, `import(` or `require(`, with optional whitespace between. Node and bundlers never expand `~` in a specifier, so this shape cannot be a home path.
- **In scope: a path-mapping key.** A quoted tilde-slash string whose last segment is exactly `*` and which is followed by optional whitespace and `:`. This is the tsconfig/jsconfig `paths` key shape.
- **Out of scope and still refused: a bare or backticked tilde-slash path in prose** (item 3 above). Nothing in the text tells it apart from a real home path like tilde, slash, `code/github.com/o/r`, which an existing test pins as refused. A filer can quote the alias inside an import line instead.
- **Rejected: the issue's non-binding idea of a list of known home directories** (`Documents/`, `code/`, `.config/`, `Library/`), or the "2+ segments ending in a filename" rule. Either one would let any unlisted real home path through (tilde, slash, `client-work/notes`). That is a looser guard, which the original rules out ("the fix has to be precise, not a looser guard"), and it is a membership list, which the contract rules out.

Triage note: `Rule.judge` only receives the match and its capture groups, not the surrounding line. So the implementer has to choose between widening the rule interface (offset plus line) and running a context-aware exemption pass before `PATH_RULE`. Either works; the criteria below pin the behaviour, not the mechanism.

Searched for an owner: `report dedup` for the leak guard and the body leak predicate found only closed, unrelated leak-guard work (email shape, private-repo names, leakNames threading). Nothing open owns this predicate, so this ticket stands alone.

Portability: the predicate and its contract ship to consumer repos. The contract text names no phoenix path or issue. Under `packages/fabrika-cli/`, the new carve-out's docblock cites this issue with an `@ruling` tag, never an ADR number or a `.decisions/` path.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `scanBody` returns no leak for a tilde-slash module specifier inside a matching quote pair directly after `from`, `import`, `import(` or `require(`, with single and double quotes each covered by a fixture in `packages/fabrika-cli/src/report/leaks.unit.test.ts`.
- [ ] `scanBody` returns no leak for a quoted tilde-slash path-mapping key whose last segment is `*` and which is followed by `:`, covered by a fixture using the tsconfig `paths` line shape.
- [ ] `scanBody` still returns exactly one `home-relative` leak for each of: a bare tilde-slash path in prose, a backticked tilde-slash path in prose, a tilde-slash home path inside quotes that follow no import keyword, and a quoted tilde-slash string ending in `/*` with no following colon. Each case is pinned by a fixture.
- [ ] A line holding both an exempt specifier and a real tilde-slash home path reports the home path as a leak, and `--redact` masks only the home path, leaving the specifier byte-for-byte intact.
- [ ] Every existing test in `leaks.unit.test.ts` passes unchanged, including the fenced-code-block refusal and the "no self-exempt list" case.
- [ ] Item 1 of "The body-surface leak predicate" in `claude-plugins/fabrika/skills/report/contract.md` names the two new shape carve-outs next to the existing claude-config carve-outs, with no phoenix-bound reference, and the `leaks.ts` docblock for the new carve-out cites this issue with an `@ruling` tag.
- [ ] `scanBody` still returns exactly one `home-relative` leak for a tilde-slash home path quoted after the word `from` or `import` in prose that is not an import/export statement (for example: copied it from, then the quoted path), pinned by a fixture in `leaks.unit.test.ts`; the module-specifier carve-out keys on code context rather than on the bare word, and item 1 of "The body-surface leak predicate" in the report contract states that narrower shape. <!-- ac:review pr:#10239 round:1 -->
- [ ] `scanBody` still returns exactly one `home-relative` leak for a tilde-slash home path quoted after the word `import` (or an `import … from` / `} from` clause) that follows a *closing* inline-code backtick in prose (for example: a backticked command name, then the word import, then the quoted path), pinned by a fixture in `leaks.unit.test.ts`; the statement anchor counts a backtick only when it opens an inline-code span, and item 1 of "The body-surface leak predicate" in the report contract says the backtick anchor is an opening one. <!-- ac:review pr:#10239 round:2 -->

---

<!-- fabrika:enriched issue=10233 mode=rewrite -->
<details>
<summary>Original report (verbatim)</summary>

## Summary

`report file`'s leak guard refuses a body that quotes a TypeScript path alias spelled with a leading tilde and slash, reading it as a home-relative machine path. The refusal is a false positive: the alias is source code, not a filesystem path, and the body had to be rewritten with a different alias spelling to post.

## What I was doing

Filing an issue about an import-resolution bug. The repro needed to quote a tsconfig `paths` entry and an import specifier that both use a tilde-slash alias (a common Next.js convention for `./src`).

## What I observed

`report file` exited 5: "the body carries 5 machine-local path(s) — refusing to post them to a public issue", listing each line as `home-relative`. Every hit was the alias in a JSON `paths` key, an import specifier in backticks, or prose naming the alias. None was a filesystem path. The workaround was to replace the alias with `@app/` in the public text and describe the real one in words, which makes the repro less exact. `--redact` would have masked the alias instead, which destroys the repro.

## Why it matters

Tilde-slash path aliases are a common default in Next.js and Vite projects, so any bug report about module resolution in such a project hits this. The guard is also correct to refuse real home paths, so the fix has to be precise, not a looser guard.

## Pointers

- `report file` and its body-surface leak predicate (`--heading "The body-surface leak predicate"` in the report contract)
- Exit 5 ("machine-local path")

## Suggested next step (non-binding)

Treat tilde-slash as a home path only when what follows looks like a filesystem path: a known home directory segment (`Documents/`, `code/`, `.config/`, `Library/`) or 2+ segments ending in a file with an extension. Don't flag it inside an import-specifier or `paths`-key shape (a quoted tilde-slash-star key, or a quoted tilde-slash specifier after `from`). Add fixtures for both.

---

ticket.body:
## In plain words

The past-target rec prints a target's hours with no unit: `past its "4h" target of 4`. Make it read as a person would say it, for example `past its "4h" target (4 hours)`, for any target name.

## Where it is, read at `origin/main`

`recOf` in `packages/fabrika-cli/src/table/flags.ts`, the `PastTarget` case:

```ts
`Open on-call for ${flag.waitedHours} hours, past its "${flag.target}" target of ${flag.hours}. Pick it up now, or move it to the table?`
```

`flag.target` is the free-form name from `boards.onCall.responseTargets` ("4h", "same day", "1 day"), and `flag.hours` is its length in hours. So a "1 day" target reads "target of 24". The existing test in `packages/fabrika-cli/src/table/flags.unit.test.ts` only checks `past its "same day" target`, so it never saw the bare number.

Triage note: #9989 is rewriting `flags.ts` and `flags-verb.ts` for the Table day change, so this one-line fix waits for it to avoid a conflict. It is a copy change only; the flag's data and when it fires stay the same. Searched for an owner (`report dedup` on the past-target rec): nothing open covers it, so it stays standalone.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `PastTarget` rec in `packages/fabrika-cli/src/table/flags.ts` shows the target's hours with a unit (for example `past its "4h" target (4 hours)`), and never a bare number after "target of".
- [ ] A unit test in `packages/fabrika-cli/src/table/flags.unit.test.ts` pins the full rec text for one target (for example "4h" at 4 hours) and shows a "1 day" target at 24 hours reads with its unit, not "target of 24".
- [ ] When and on which items the past-target flag fires is unchanged: the existing past-target tests pass as they stand.

---

ticket.body:
## The decision

May a `Program.shape` name a request port at all — and if so, does the shape declare both halves of
that port's contract?

Today `ProgramShape` is exactly `{in, out}` (`apps/tuval/src/authoring/shape.ts`). A `request` port
declares two schemas, `input` and `output` (`apps/tuval/src/authoring/port.ts`, `declareRequest`),
and the fit check reads only the first:

```ts
const inSignature = (decl: AnyPortDecl): PortCodec<any> | undefined =>
	decl.direction === "in" ? decl.schema : decl.direction === "request" ? decl.input : undefined;
```

`decl.output` is read nowhere in `shape.ts`. `fitsShape` compares in-side against in-side and
out-side against out-side, so no path in the check can reach a request port's reply schema. A shape
declaring `{in: {ask: Prompt}}` therefore fits any program whose `ask` is a request taking `Prompt`
and answering anything at all.

## Why it is a decision and not a bug

`{in, out}` does exactly what it says, so nothing here violates a "supposed to" — the vocabulary has
no way to express "and it answers this", and folding a request onto the in side is what makes the
reply schema unreachable. Picking the direction is the deliverable, and the two candidates change
the public authoring API differently:

- **A third key.** `ProgramShape` grows something like `ask: {name: {input, output}}`, with its own
  side in `ShapeSide` and its own `ShapeMismatch` reason. A request stops being an in-port. Costs a
  new key on a surface authors write by hand.
- **Leave `{in, out}` as the whole vocabulary**, and make the omission loud instead of silent — a
  shape that names a port the program declares as a request is refused, rather than half-checked.
  Keeps the two-key surface; a shaped arg then simply cannot ask.

A third option worth naming so it is rejected on purpose: extend the in-side comparison to also
match `output`. That keeps the key count but leaves a request declared under `in`, which is the
framing that hid the reply schema.

## What is at stake, and what is not

The check exists so a config filling a program-valued arg with the wrong program is refused at the
fill site, naming the port. A request port slips half its contract past that refusal, so the
mismatch surfaces later as a decode failure on the reply, away from the config line that caused it.

Nothing in the tree fills a shaped arg with a request-porting program today, so there is no live
victim. The code above is not on `main` — it lives on the open epic PR
https://github.com/kamp-us/phoenix/pull/8750 for epic #8716, and #8729's `review-code` verdict
(comment id 5600565835) named this under "Non-blocking observations", outside that issue's
acceptance criteria. Read the branch, not `main`, to see it.

Triage note: I read `shape.ts` and `port.ts` at `origin/epic/8716` and confirmed `decl.output` has no
reader in `shape.ts` and that `fitsShape` only ever calls `fitSide` on `in` and `out`. Both
candidates above are my reading of the fork the filer described; neither is a founder ruling.

Triage note: nothing on the board owns this question. Searched for the surface — #8726 declares the
port vocabulary (`port.in`/`out`/`request`), #8729 introduces `Program.shape`, epic #8716 scopes the
authoring API to `{in, out}` at R15.1. None of the three asks whether a shape may name a request, so
this is minted standalone rather than folded into a ticket whose PR is already in review.

Triage note: homed on the `wayfinder:backlog` lane, not milestone 55. Milestone 55 (Tuval programs)
is an active campaign's milestone and closed to new `p2` intake, and this is a `p2` — pre-release
API, no consumer, no live victim.

## The ruling

Ruled 2026-09-10 (EA session on the founder's behalf, under the standing #8807 R4.1 grant that
engine and repo-hygiene calls are the driver's): **option B**. A shape keeps the two-key
`{in, out}` vocabulary, and a shape that names a port the program declares as a `request` is
**refused** rather than half-checked. The third option — extending the in-side comparison to also
match `output` — is rejected on purpose: it keeps the key count but leaves a request declared under
`in`, which is the framing that hid the reply schema in the first place.

Ruling comment: https://github.com/kamp-us/phoenix/issues/8770#issuecomment-5625040922

The work sits in the same file family as #8746 and #8749, so one pass over
`apps/tuval/src/authoring/shape.ts` covers all three where practical.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `inSignature` in `apps/tuval/src/authoring/shape.ts` no longer folds a `request` port's
      `input` onto the in side — a `request` declaration contributes no signature to either side of
      `shapeOf`.
- [ ] `fitsShape` refuses, rather than silently passing, when a declared shape names a port the
      candidate program declares as `request`: the failure is a `ShapeMismatch` naming that `port`,
      carrying `side: "in"`, and a `reason` that says the program declares that port as a request
      and a shape cannot name one.
- [ ] The public authoring surface is unchanged: `ProgramShape` still has exactly `in` and `out`,
      `ShapeSide` still has exactly `"in" | "out"`, and no third key or new side is added.
- [ ] The in-side comparison is **not** extended to match a request's `output`; a note at the
      refusal site in `shape.ts` records that the reply schema is deliberately unreachable from a
      shape and why folding a request under `in` was rejected.
- [ ] `apps/tuval/src/authoring/shape.unit.test.ts` covers both halves: a shape naming a port the
      program declares `request` is refused with the `ShapeMismatch` above, and the same shape
      against a program declaring that port as a genuine `in` port of the same payload still fits.
- [ ] `pnpm typecheck` passes and the `apps/tuval` authoring unit tests pass.

---

<details>
<summary>Original report (verbatim)</summary>

## Summary
`Program.shape` types a program-valued arg by its `{in, out}` port signatures. A `request` port is
read onto the in side by its input schema alone, and the reply schema is never compared on either
side. So a shape declaring an in-port fits a program whose port of that name is a request returning
anything at all, and the author never finds out until the reply arrives.

## What I was doing
Repairing the `review-code` FAIL on #8729, which built `apps/tuval/src/authoring/shape.ts`. The
reviewer named this beside the two blocking findings as a non-blocking observation, outside that
issue's acceptance criteria, so the repair round did not touch it.

## What I observed
In `apps/tuval/src/authoring/shape.ts`:

```ts
const inSignature = (decl: AnyPortDecl): PortCodec<any> | undefined =>
	decl.direction === "in" ? decl.schema : decl.direction === "request" ? decl.input : undefined;
```

`decl.output` is read nowhere. `fitsShape` then only compares in-side against in-side and out-side
against out-side, so nothing in the check can ever reach a request port's reply schema.

The shape vocabulary has no way to say "and it answers this" either: `ProgramShape` is exactly
`{in, out}` and a request is neither. So this is a limit of the vocabulary rather than a bug in the
comparison — but it is silent, and a shape author reading `Program.shape({in: {ask: Prompt}})` would
reasonably read it as a promise about the whole port.

## Why it matters
The check exists so a config that fills a program-valued arg with the wrong program is refused at
the fill site, naming the port. A request port slips half of its contract past that refusal, which
means a mismatch that could have been caught by the config surfaces instead as a runtime decode
failure on the reply, at a distance from the config line that caused it.

Uncertainty: nothing in the tree fills a shaped arg with a request-porting program today, so this
has no live victim yet. Whether it needs fixing turns on whether the `{in, out}` vocabulary is meant
to stay that shape — that is a design question for the epic, not obviously a defect.

## Pointers
- `apps/tuval/src/authoring/shape.ts` — `inSignature`, `outSignature`, `ProgramShape`, `fitsShape`
- `apps/tuval/src/authoring/port.ts` — `port.request(input, output)`
- https://github.com/kamp-us/phoenix/issues/8729 — the `review-code` verdict comment
  (id 5600565835), under "Non-blocking observations"
- Epic https://github.com/kamp-us/phoenix/issues/8716

## Suggested next step (non-binding)
A guess: decide first whether a shape should be able to name a request at all. If yes, that is a
third key on `ProgramShape` (something like `ask: {name: {input, output}}`) rather than a change to
the in-side comparison, since a request is not an in-port and folding it into one is what hid the
reply schema in the first place.

---

ticket.body:
## What is wrong

ADR 0402 rule 7 now names a closed set: boot's one-time move takes `manifest.json`, `processes/`
and `pi-sessions/` out of `<project>/.tuval`, and leaves the config module **and every other entry
it does not recognise** where it is. That wording landed with PR #9612, recording the founder's
ruling on #9566.

`adoptInProjectState` in `apps/tuval/src/state-dir.ts` still moves by exclusion. Read at
`origin/main`, the loop skips one name and lifts everything else:

```ts
for (const entry of entries) {
	if (entry === CONFIG_MODULE) continue;
	const target = join(stateDir, entry);
	if (yield* fs.exists(target)) {
		kept.push(entry);
		continue;
	}
	yield* lift(join(projectTuvalDir, entry), target);
	moved.push(entry);
}
```

So a note, a scratch file, or any second file an operator parked in that directory is relocated
into the home-dir key on the next boot. The record and the code disagree, and the record is the one
the founder ruled.

## What has to change

- The membership test inverts: move an entry when its name is in the closed set, leave every other
  name alone. `CONFIG_MODULE` stops being a special case — it is simply a name outside the set.
- `StateAdoption` in the same module carries two reasons to leave something behind, and today only
  one. `kept` means "the home-dir key already holds this name"; "Tuval does not own this name" is a
  different fact and reporting both under `kept` reads as one. The interface needs a third field,
  and `BootReport.adopted` in `apps/tuval/src/boot.ts` carries it through unchanged.
- `apps/tuval/src/bin.ts` prints the adoption report. Its second line today reads
  `left … — <stateDir> already holds one of each`, which is only true of the collision arm; the
  not-ours arm needs its own line with its own reason.
- The module docblock at the top of `apps/tuval/src/state-dir.ts` states the exclusion shape
  ("lifts everything else out of it once and leaves that module behind"), and so does
  `adoptInProjectState`'s own docblock. Both move with the loop.

Triage note: the accepted cost is the founder's, stated in his ruling — a future kind of Tuval
state file has to be added to the set by hand. That is the trade, not a gap to design around.

Triage note: nothing on the board owns this surface. #9566, #9537 and #9515 are the ruling and its
predecessors and are all closed; milestone 54 is the campaign this belongs to, not an owning
ticket. Minted standalone.

## Where the work is

- `apps/tuval/src/state-dir.ts` — `adoptInProjectState`, `CONFIG_MODULE`, `StateAdoption`
- `apps/tuval/src/state-dir.unit.test.ts` — the existing `the one-time move of in-project state`
  suite, which already covers the re-run and collision arms
- `apps/tuval/src/boot.ts` — `BootReport.adopted`
- `apps/tuval/src/bin.ts` — the `moved` and `left` boot lines
- `.decisions/0402-tuval-state-lives-under-home.md` — rule 7 and its amendment

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `adoptInProjectState` moves an entry only when its name is `manifest.json`, `processes/` or `pi-sessions/`; a unit test seeds an unrecognised entry beside a recognised one under the project's `.tuval` and asserts the unrecognised entry is still at its original path after the call, and absent from the state dir.
- [ ] `tuval.config.ts` is never moved, and is left by the same rule as any other unrecognised name rather than by a name-specific skip — a unit test asserts it stays put with no `CONFIG_MODULE` special case left in the loop.
- [ ] `StateAdoption` reports the two reasons for leaving an entry behind under separate fields: one for a name the home-dir key already holds, one for a name Tuval does not own. A unit test seeds both cases in one directory and asserts each entry comes back under its own field.
- [ ] `apps/tuval/src/bin.ts` prints a distinct line per reason, each stating that reason, and prints neither line when its field is empty.
- [ ] The existing `the one-time move of in-project state` tests still pass unchanged in meaning: a second call moves nothing, a project with no `.tuval` reports empty, and an entry the state dir already holds is not overwritten.
- [ ] The module docblock and `adoptInProjectState`'s docblock in `apps/tuval/src/state-dir.ts` describe the closed set rather than the exclusion, and cite ADR 0402 rule 7.

---

<!-- fabrika:enriched issue=9611 mode=rewrite -->
<details>
<summary>Original report (verbatim)</summary>

## Summary

The founder ruled on #9566 that Tuval's one-time move of in-project state takes only what Tuval
itself wrote — `manifest.json`, `processes/` and `pi-sessions/` — and leaves everything else in
`<project>/.tuval` untouched. `adoptInProjectState` still moves by exclusion: it lifts every entry
except `tuval.config.ts`. ADR 0402's rule 7 now records the ruling; the code does not yet follow it.

## What I was doing

Building #9566, whose deliverable is the amendment to ADR 0402 rule 7 recording that ruling. The
issue's third acceptance criterion asks for this follow-up where the pick differs from today's loop,
and it does differ.

## What I observed

`adoptInProjectState` in `apps/tuval/src/state-dir.ts`, at `origin/main`:

```ts
for (const entry of entries) {
	if (entry === CONFIG_MODULE) continue;
	const target = join(stateDir, entry);
	if (yield* fs.exists(target)) {
		kept.push(entry);
		continue;
	}
	yield* lift(join(projectTuvalDir, entry), target);
	moved.push(entry);
}
```

Anything an operator left in that directory that is not Tuval state — notes, a scratch file, a
second config the loader does not read — is moved into the home-dir key. The ruled behaviour is the
inverse test: move an entry when its name is one of the three Tuval writes, and leave every other
name where it is, named on the boot's `left` line so the operator can see what was skipped.

The module's docblock also states the exclusion shape ("lifts everything else out of it once and
leaves that module behind"), so it moves with the loop. The `StateAdoption` interface's `kept` field
today means "the home-dir key already holds this name"; a not-ours entry is a different reason to
leave something behind, and reporting the two under one name would read as one fact.

## Why it matters

Low frequency and the blast radius is a file moved rather than destroyed, but the ruling is exactly
about a directory Tuval does not own: on the work repository ADR 0402 exists for, a boot rewriting
an operator's own files without asking is the surprise the founder ruled out. Until this lands, the
ADR and the code disagree, and the ADR is the one that is right.

## Pointers

- `apps/tuval/src/state-dir.ts` — `adoptInProjectState`, `CONFIG_MODULE`, `StateAdoption`
- `apps/tuval/src/bin.ts` — the `moved` and `left` boot lines
- `.decisions/0402-tuval-state-lives-under-home.md` — rule 7 and its 2026-09-20 amendment
- #9566 (the decision and its ruling comment), #9537, PR #9555

## Suggested next step (non-binding)

A guess: replace the `CONFIG_MODULE` skip with a closed set of the three names Tuval writes, report
an unrecognised entry on the boot's `left` line distinctly from an entry the home-dir key already
holds, and cover both arms in the existing state-dir unit tests. The accepted cost, stated in the
